Open `GWAS_course.Rproj` and work from the project root. Run the chunks in order in a fresh R session.
All data are simulated. Read each summary, run its chunk and compare your result with the expected result.
The linked step pages explain the ideas and provide troubleshooting.

::: {.callout-note title="In this module"}

**Time.** About 70 minutes.

**Before you start.** You need the full [checkpoint at step 2.8](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-2/step-2-8). The first code chunk checks the files that this module needs.

**Steps.**

- [3.1 Rough cleaning](#step-3-1)
- [3.2 Sample call rate](#step-3-2)
- [3.3 Recorded and genetic sex](#step-3-3)
- [3.4 LD pruning](#step-3-4)
- [3.5 Heterozygosity](#step-3-5)
- [3.6 Relatedness and duplicates](#step-3-6)
- [3.7 Batch effects](#step-3-7)
- [3.8 Sample QC summary and checkpoint](#step-3-8)

**Where the module ends.** The checkpoint at step 3.8.

:::

#| label: module3_check

## Step 3.1 · Rough cleaning {#step-3-1}

We remove samples and variants with very many missing calls. This first clean prevents the worst failures from distorting the checks that follow.

[Read step 3.1 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-1).

```{r}
#| label: s3-1
input <- guided_path(cfg, "2.8")  # <1>
rough <- guided_path(cfg, "3.1", "samples")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", input, "--mind", "0.10", "--make-pgen", "--out", rough))  # <2>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", rough, "--geno", "0.10", "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.1")))  # <3>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.1", "2.8")
guided_register(cfg, "3.1", "2.8", 2013, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Choose the input files and the names for the saved files.
2. Remove samples with more than 10% of calls missing.
3. Remove variants with more than 10% of calls missing.

### What each option does

**Command 1: remove poor samples**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--mind` | Removes samples with more than 10% missing calls. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 2: remove poor variants**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--geno` | Removes variants with more than 10% missing calls in the input dataset. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Three wells and 150 variants are removed. 2,013 samples and 296,360 variants remain.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s2-8_state --mind 0.10 --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-1_samples --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-1_samples --geno 0.10 --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-1_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

Each trial changes one limit and starts from the same input as the step.

**Chart: --mind.**

**Why this simulation.** The first clean removes broken wells before the finer checks. How generous should the call rate limit be?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one value of `--mind`, the largest share of missing calls that a sample may have. The vertical axis counts the samples removed, and the diamond is the course value.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.2**. The count equals the one at the course value.
- Change it to **0.01**. Many more samples are removed.

**What you should see, and why.** A few wells are so poor that every generous limit removes them. Stricter limits remove good wells too.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.1](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-1) is a rough first clean. Finer checks follow in [step 3.2](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-2) and [step 4.1](../lessons/module_04_variant_quality_control.Rmd#step-4-1), so it can be generous.

**Key idea:** A generous first clean removes only broken wells and leaves the fine decisions to later steps.

**Chart: --geno.**

**Why this simulation.** The same question for variants: how generous should the first variant filter be?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one value of `--geno`, the largest share of missing calls that a variant may have. The vertical axis counts the variants removed.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.01**. Many more variants are removed.
- Change it to **0.2**. Fewer variants are removed.

**What you should see, and why.** Many variants have a little missing data, so a strict limit removes many sites. The generous course value removes only the clearly broken ones.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 4.1](../lessons/module_04_variant_quality_control.Rmd#step-4-1) applies a stricter variant filter after the sample checks, so this one can stay generous.

**Key idea:** Variants can be removed later, so the first filter is generous.

```{r}
#| label: s3-1_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. Each trial starts from the same input and changes one threshold only. Your results folder is not changed.
thresholds <- c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
samples <- threshold_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "2.8"), "--mind", thresholds)  # <1>
samples$course_value <- samples$threshold == 0.10
samples
variants <- threshold_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.1", "samples"), "--geno", thresholds)  # <2>
variants$course_value <- variants$threshold == 0.10
variants
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot_threshold_trials(samples, "Samples removed"); plot_threshold_trials(variants, "Variants removed")  # <3>
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```

1. Samples: --mind on the cohort saved at 2.8.
2. Variants: --geno on the samples that remain after --mind 0.10.
3. Plot the removed numbers. The course value is the large diamond.


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s2-8_state --mind 0.05 --make-just-psam --out results/trials/s3-1_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

The log file `results/trials/s3-1_trial.log` states how many samples were removed. To repeat the trial, change the number after `--mind` and use a new `--out` name. For variants, use `--geno` and `--make-just-pvar` on `s3-1_samples`.

The expected result of the trials:

Samples removed by `--mind`:

| Threshold | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.01 | 121 | 1,895 |
| 0.02 | 45 | 1,971 |
| 0.05 | 3 | 2,013 |
| **0.1 (course value)** | 3 | 2,013 |
| 0.2 | 3 | 2,013 |

Variants removed by `--geno`, after `--mind 0.10`:

| Threshold | Variants removed | Variants remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.01 | 3,705 | 292,805 |
| 0.02 | 958 | 295,552 |
| 0.05 | 735 | 295,775 |
| **0.1 (course value)** | 150 | 296,360 |
| 0.2 | 130 | 296,380 |

:::

## Step 3.2 · Sample call rate {#step-3-2}

We remove samples with more than 2% of their genotype calls missing. This keeps samples with enough information for the later analysis.

[Read step 3.2 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-2).

```{r}
#| label: s3-2
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.1"), "--mind", "0.02", "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.2")))  # <1>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.2", "3.1")
guided_register(cfg, "3.2", "3.1", 1971, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Remove samples with more than 2% of calls missing.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--mind` | Removes samples with more than 2% missing calls, keeping a call rate of at least 98%. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

42 more wells are removed. 1,971 samples and 296,360 variants remain.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-1_state --mind 0.02 --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-2_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

Each trial starts from the cohort saved at 3.1 and changes the limit only.

**Chart: --mind.**

**Why this simulation.** A sample with many missing calls has poor DNA or a poor genotyping well. Where should the call rate limit be?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one `--mind` value: samples with more than that share of missing calls are removed. The vertical axis counts the samples removed, and the diamond is the course value.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.05**. The count falls, because poor but not broken wells stay.
- Change it to **0.01**. Many more samples are removed.

**What you should see, and why.** The course value removes wells that are poor but not broken. A looser limit lets them in. A stricter limit throws away good data.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.2](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-2) decides which samples enter every later step. Poor samples add noise.

**Key idea:** A call rate limit trades sample size against data quality.

```{r}
#| label: s3-2_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. Each trial starts from the same input and changes one threshold only.
thresholds <- c(0.01, 0.02, 0.05, 0.10, 0.20)
trial <- threshold_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.1"), "--mind", thresholds)
trial$course_value <- trial$threshold == 0.02
trial
# Plot the removed samples. The course value is the large diamond.
plot_threshold_trials(trial, "Samples removed")
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-1_state --mind 0.05 --make-just-psam --out results/trials/s3-2_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

The log file `results/trials/s3-2_trial.log` states how many samples were removed. To repeat the trial, change the number after `--mind` and use a new `--out` name.

The expected result of the trials:

| Threshold | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.01 | 118 | 1,895 |
| **0.02 (course value)** | 42 | 1,971 |
| 0.05 | 0 | 2,013 |
| 0.1 | 0 | 2,013 |
| 0.2 | 0 | 2,013 |

:::

## Step 3.3 · Recorded and genetic sex {#step-3-3}

We compare recorded sex with patterns in the X and Y chromosome calls. We remove flagged wells from this teaching analysis because a mismatch needs review before the sample is used.

[Read step 3.3 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-3).

```{r}
#| label: s3-3
split <- guided_path(cfg, "3.3", "par")  # <1>
report <- guided_path(cfg, "3.3", "sexcheck")
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.2"), "--split-par", "b38", "--make-pgen", "--out", split))  # <2>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", split, "--check-sex", "max-female-xf=0.2", "min-male-xf=0.8",  # <3>
  "max-female-ycount=100", "min-male-ycount=1000", "--out", report))
sexcheck <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".sexcheck"))  # <4>
bad <- sexcheck$IID[sexcheck$STATUS != "OK"]
remove_file <- guided_list(bad, guided_path(cfg, "3.3", "remove.txt"), TRUE)
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", split, "--remove", remove_file, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.3")))  # <5>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.3", "3.2", extra = data.frame(option = "--split-par", value = "b38"))
guided_register(cfg, "3.3", "3.2", 1963, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Choose names for the chromosome files and sex report.
2. Label the regions shared by the X and Y chromosomes.
3. Compare recorded sex with the X and Y chromosome results.
4. Read the report and list samples that need to be removed.
5. Save the dataset without the flagged samples.

### What each option does

**Command 1: label the shared X and Y regions**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--split-par` | Uses GRCh38 boundaries (b38) to label the shared regions of X and Y separately. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 2: compare recorded sex with DNA**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--check-sex` | Compares recorded sex with X chromosome patterns and the number of observed Y calls. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `max-female-xf` | Sets 0.2 as the largest accepted X chromosome F value for a recorded female. F measures how homozygous the X chromosome looks, meaning how often the two copies carry the same DNA letter. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `min-male-xf` | Sets 0.8 as the smallest accepted X chromosome F value for a recorded male. F measures how homozygous the X chromosome looks. Values near 1 are expected when there is only one X chromosome, as in males. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `max-female-ycount` | Accepts at most 100 observed Y calls for a recorded female. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `min-male-ycount` | Requires at least 1000 observed Y calls for a recorded male. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 3: remove samples flagged by the sex check**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--remove` | Removes the samples named in the supplied sample list. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Eight flagged wells are removed. 1,963 samples remain. 520 sites are labelled PAR1 or PAR2. The number of variants does not change.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-2_state --split-par b38 --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-3_par --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_par --check-sex max-female-xf=0.2 min-male-xf=0.8 max-female-ycount=100 min-male-ycount=1000 --out results/guided/s3-3_sexcheck --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_par --remove results/guided/s3-3_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-3_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

Each trial changes one limit of the sex check.

**Chart: max-female-xf.**

**Why this simulation.** The sex check flags samples whose X chromosome does not fit the recorded sex. How strict should the female limit be?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one value of `max-female-xf`, the highest X inbreeding coefficient (F) that a recorded female may have. Females have F near 0, males near 1. The vertical axis counts the samples removed, and the diamond is the course value.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.1**. More samples are flagged.
- Change it to **0.4**. The count equals the one at the course value.

**What you should see, and why.** A strict limit flags females whose F is only a little above 0, who may be real females with noisy data. Above the course value, the flagged samples are far from the limit: probably mismatches or swaps.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.3](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-3) removes samples whose X data contradict the recorded sex. A mismatch often means a swapped sample.

**Key idea:** Clear mismatches survive any sensible limit, and only borderline samples depend on it.

**Chart: min-male-xf.**

**Why this simulation.** Same question for males: how low may F be for a recorded male?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one value of `min-male-xf`, the lowest F that a recorded male may have. Axes and diamond are as above.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.6**. Note the count.
- Change it to **0.9**. The count is the same.

**What you should see, and why.** The count does not change, so the recorded males lie far from the limit. In this dataset the exact male limit does not matter.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** In [step 3.3](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-3) you can keep the course limit for males.

**Key idea:** When a limit changes nothing, the exact value does not matter.

```{r}
#| label: s3-3_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. Each trial starts from the same input and changes one limit only. Your results folder is not changed.
females <- sexcheck_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.3", "par"), "max-female-xf", c(0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4))  # <1>
females$course_value <- females$threshold == 0.2
males <- sexcheck_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.3", "par"), "min-male-xf", c(0.6, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9))  # <2>
males$course_value <- males$threshold == 0.8
females
males
par(mfrow = c(1, 2)); plot_threshold_trials(females, "Samples flagged", log_x = FALSE); plot_threshold_trials(males, "Samples flagged", log_x = FALSE)  # <3>
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```

1. Change the female limit, with the other limits at their course values.
2. Change the male limit.
3. Plot the flagged samples. The course value is the large diamond.


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_par --check-sex max-female-xf=0.3 min-male-xf=0.8 max-female-ycount=100 min-male-ycount=1000 --out results/trials/s3-3_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

Count the rows of `results/trials/s3-3_trial.sexcheck` whose `STATUS` is not `OK`. To repeat the trial, change one number and use a new `--out` name.

The expected result of the trials:

Samples flagged when the female limit changes:

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1 | 14 | 1,957 |
| **0.2 (course value)** | 8 | 1,963 |
| 0.3 | 8 | 1,963 |
| 0.4 | 8 | 1,963 |

Samples flagged when the male limit changes:

| Setting | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.6 | 8 | 1,963 |
| 0.7 | 8 | 1,963 |
| **0.8 (course value)** | 8 | 1,963 |
| 0.9 | 8 | 1,963 |

:::

## Step 3.4 · LD pruning {#step-3-4}

We select common DNA sites that are less strongly correlated with each other. This stops groups of similar sites from weighing too much in the sample checks. The full dataset is kept for the association scan.

[Read step 3.4 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-4).

```{r}
#| label: s3-4
regions <- guided_high_ld(cfg)  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.3"), "--chr", "1-22", "--maf", "0.05", "--geno", "0.02",  # <2>
  "--exclude", "bed0", regions, "--indep-pairwise", "200kb", "0.2", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.4", "prune")))
pruned <- readLines(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.4", "prune"), ".prune.in"))  # <3>
stopifnot(length(pruned) == 68800L)
cat(length(pruned), "variants kept by LD pruning\n")
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
guided_artifact_checkpoint(cfg, "3.4", c(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.4", "prune"), c(".prune.in", ".prune.out")), regions), parent = "3.3")
```

1. Write the list of regions where nearby variants are strongly correlated.
2. Select variants with less similar patterns of DNA letters.
3. Check and print how many variants were selected.

### What each option does

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--chr` | Uses only chromosomes 1 to 22, the autosomes. |
| `--maf` | Keeps variants whose less common allele has a frequency of at least 5%. |
| `--geno` | Keeps variants with no more than 2% missing calls. |
| `--exclude` | Leaves out variants within the listed DNA regions. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `bed0` | Reads DNA regions in the BED way: the start of each region is counted from 0 and its end is not included. |
| `--indep-pairwise` | Compares genotype patterns at pairs of sites within windows of 200 kb (200,000 DNA bases). It drops one site of every pair with a squared correlation (r²) above 0.2. A larger r² means that the genotypes of the two sites vary together more closely. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

The `.prune.in` file lists 68,800 sites. The complete analysis state still has 296,360 variants.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_state --chr 1-22 --maf 0.05 --geno 0.02 --exclude bed0 results/guided/s3-4_high_ld.bed0 --indep-pairwise 200kb 0.2 --out results/guided/s3-4_prune --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

Each trial changes one setting of LD pruning. Here "removed" means pruned out.

**Chart: r2 limit.**

**Why this simulation.** LD pruning drops one variant of each correlated pair. How strict should the correlation limit be?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one r2 limit, the squared correlation above which one variant of a pair is dropped. The vertical axis counts the variants pruned out, and the diamond marks the course value.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.1**. More variants are dropped.
- Change it to **0.5**. Fewer variants are dropped.

**What you should see, and why.** A low limit counts weaker correlations as pairs, so it drops more variants. A high limit keeps pairs of similar variants, which then count twice in the PCA.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.4](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-4) makes the variant list that the next checks and the PCA use. Too many correlated variants overweight some regions, and too few lose information.

**Key idea:** Pruning trades independence against information, and the course takes a middle value.

**Chart: window (kb).**

**Why this simulation.** The window is how far apart two variants may be and still be compared. Does it matter as much?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one window length in kb. The axes and the diamond are as above.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **50**. Note the count.
- Change it to **1000**. The count changes less than it did for the r2 limit.

**What you should see, and why.** A wider window finds more pairs, but the count changes much less than for the r2 limit, because correlation fades with distance.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** In [step 3.4](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-4) you can keep the course window. The r2 limit is the setting that decides how many variants you keep.

**Key idea:** The window matters less than the r2 limit.

```{r}
#| label: s3-4_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. Each trial starts from the same input and changes one setting only. It writes no file in your results folder.
regions <- guided_high_ld(cfg)
r2_limits <- c(0.1, 0.2, 0.5)  # <1>
by_r2 <- sapply(r2_limits, function(r) prune_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.3"), regions, r2 = r, window_kb = 200))
windows <- c(50, 200, 1000)  # <2>
by_window <- sapply(windows, function(w) prune_counts(cfg, guided_path(cfg, "3.3"), regions, r2 = 0.2, window_kb = w))
data.frame(r2 = r2_limits, kept = by_r2["kept", ], pruned = by_r2["pruned", ])
data.frame(window_kb = windows, kept = by_window["kept", ], pruned = by_window["pruned", ])
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))  # <3>
plot_threshold_trials(data.frame(threshold = r2_limits, removed = by_r2["pruned", ], course_value = r2_limits == 0.2), "Variants pruned out", log_x = FALSE)
plot_threshold_trials(data.frame(threshold = windows, removed = by_window["pruned", ], course_value = windows == 200), "Variants pruned out")
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```

1. Change the r2 limit, with a window of 200 kb.
2. Change the window, with an r2 limit of 0.2.
3. Plot the pruned variants. The course value is the large diamond.


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_state --chr 1-22 --maf 0.05 --geno 0.02 --exclude bed0 results/guided/s3-4_high_ld.bed0 --indep-pairwise 200kb 0.5 --out results/trials/s3-4_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

Count the lines of `results/trials/s3-4_trial.prune.in`: it is the number of variants kept.

The expected result of the trials:

Variants pruned out and kept when the r^2 limit changes (window 200 kb):

| Setting | Variants removed | Variants remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.1 | 76,459 | 48,602 |
| **0.2 (course value)** | 56,261 | 68,800 |
| 0.5 | 24,308 | 100,753 |

Variants pruned out and kept when the window changes (r^2 limit 0.2):

| Setting | Variants removed | Variants remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 50 | 46,961 | 78,100 |
| **200 (course value)** | 56,261 | 68,800 |
| 1000 | 57,375 | 67,686 |

:::

This optional box is not part of the main path. No later step uses it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Deep dive: what happens if the long-range LD regions stay in?" collapse="true"}

**The idea.** A principal component should describe differences between people across the whole genome. In a region with a long stretch of strongly correlated variants, one pattern repeats over thousands of sites. A PC can then describe that one region instead of the ancestry of the people. This is why this step leaves such regions out before the PCA.

**Where to see it.** You cannot see this effect yet, because the PCs are calculated in module 5. The optional deep dive "Can one region take over a PC?" in step 5.7 does the experiment on your own data. It calculates the PCs with and without the list of regions, and it plots the loadings along the genome. A loading tells how much a variant contributes to a PC.

**Quick check.** Why do we leave the regions out before the PCA, and not only before the association scan?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

The regions disturb the PCs, and the PCs are then used as covariates in the scan. The association scan itself still uses all the variants that pass quality control.

</details>

**Reference.** Price et al. 2008 ([doi:10.1016/j.ajhg.2008.06.005](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ajhg.2008.06.005)) describe long-range LD that can confound genome scans in admixed populations. Privé et al. 2020 ([doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btaa520)) report that some PCs capture LD structure and not population structure.

:::

## Step 3.5 · Heterozygosity {#step-3-5}

We check whether each sample has unusually many or few sites with two different DNA letters. We remove samples with unusually many such sites and flag those with unusually few for review, because an unusual value alone does not prove an error.

[Read step 3.5 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-5).

```{r}
#| label: s3-5
report <- guided_path(cfg, "3.5", "het")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.3"), "--extract", paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.4", "prune"), ".prune.in"), "--het", "--out", report))  # <2>
het <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".het"))  # <3>
f <- as.numeric(het$F)
mean_f <- mean(f); sd_f <- sqrt(mean((f - mean_f)^2))
low <- het$IID[f < mean_f - 3 * sd_f]  # <4>
high <- het$IID[f > mean_f + 3 * sd_f]
guided_list(high, guided_path(cfg, "3.5", "flag_high.txt"), TRUE)  # <5>
remove_file <- guided_list(low, guided_path(cfg, "3.5", "remove.txt"), TRUE)
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.3"), "--remove", remove_file, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.5")))  # <6>
print(c(mean_F = mean_f, SD_F = sd_f))  # <7>
print(c(low_removed = length(low), high_flagged = length(high)))
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.5", "3.3")
guided_register(cfg, "3.5", "3.4", 1950, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Choose the name for the report of matching DNA letters.
2. Measure matching DNA letters using the selected variants.
3. Read the report and calculate the average and spread of F.
4. Find samples with unusually low or high F values.
5. Save the high F review list and the low F removal list.
6. Save the dataset without the low F samples.
7. Print the average and spread of F, then the numbers of flagged samples as whole numbers.

### What each option does

**Command 1: measure matching DNA letters**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--extract` | Uses only the variants named in the supplied variant list. |
| `--het` | Reports, for each sample, the observed and expected numbers of genotypes with two matching DNA letters, and calculates F from them. R reads the F values and calculates the review thresholds. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 2: remove samples with unusually high heterozygosity**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--remove` | Removes the samples named in the supplied sample list. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

13 wells with low F are removed. Eight wells with high F are flagged and kept. The mean F is approximately 0.0078. The population SD is approximately 0.0298. 1,950 samples remain.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_state --extract results/guided/s3-4_prune.prune.in --het --out results/guided/s3-5_het --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_state --remove results/guided/s3-5_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-5_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

The trials change the number of standard deviations (SD) and use the same F values.

**Chart: F cutoff (standard deviations).**

**Why this simulation.** Samples with too many heterozygous calls may be contaminated. How many SD below the mean should the course remove?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one SD limit for the F statistic, which compares the homozygosity that we see in a sample with the one that we expect. A very low F means too many heterozygous calls. The vertical axis counts the samples removed, and the diamond marks the course value.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **2**. Note the count.
- Change it to **4**. The count is the same.

**What you should see, and why.** The same group is removed at every limit from 2 to 4 SD, so it is clearly separate from the rest of the samples.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.5](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-5) removes samples with too many heterozygous calls, a sign of contamination, which would add false genotypes.

**Key idea:** A clear outlier group does not depend on the exact SD limit.

```{r}
#| label: s3-5_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. The trials use the table of F values that the step wrote. No PLINK run is needed.
multipliers <- c(2, 2.5, 3, 3.5, 4)
trial <- het_counts(guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.5", "het"), ".het")), multipliers)
trial$course_value <- trial$threshold == 3
trial
# Plot the removed samples. The course value is the large diamond.
plot_threshold_trials(trial, "Samples removed", log_x = FALSE)
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-3_state --extract results/guided/s3-4_prune.prune.in --het --out results/trials/s3-5_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

The command writes the F table (`results/trials/s3-5_trial.het`). The course calculates the limit in R from this table.

The expected result of the trials:

| SD from the mean | Samples removed | Samples remaining | Samples flagged |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 2 | 13 | 1,950 | 13 |
| 2.5 | 13 | 1,950 | 11 |
| **3 (course value)** | 13 | 1,950 | 8 |
| 3.5 | 13 | 1,950 | 5 |
| 4 | 13 | 1,950 | 0 |

:::

## Step 3.6 · Relatedness and duplicates {#step-3-6}

We compare pairs of samples to find repeated measurements and close relatives. We apply the stated removal rules, and keep the person with the better call rate, so that repeated or closely related people do not distort the later association analysis.

[Read step 3.6 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-6).

```{r}
#| label: s3-6
report <- guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "king")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.5"), "--extract", paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.4", "prune"), ".prune.in"),  # <2>
  "--make-king-table", "--king-table-filter", "0.0442", "--out", report))
kin <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".kin0"))  # <3>
kin <- kin[order(-as.numeric(kin$KINSHIP)), ]
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)  # <4>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.5"), "--missing", "sample-only", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "missing")))
sample_missing <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "missing"), ".smiss"))
lower_call_rate <- function(a, b) {
  fa <- as.numeric(sample_missing$F_MISS[match(a, sample_missing$IID)]); fb <- as.numeric(sample_missing$F_MISS[match(b, sample_missing$IID)])
  if (fa > fb) a else if (fb > fa) b else max(a, b)
}
remove <- character()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(kin))) {  # <5>
  a <- kin$IID1[i]; b <- kin$IID2[i]; value <- as.numeric(kin$KINSHIP[i])
  if (value > 0.354) {  # <6>
    if (endsWith(a, "_R2") || endsWith(b, "_R2")) {  # <7>
      remove <- union(remove, if (endsWith(a, "_R2")) a else b)
    } else {
      ai <- match(a, metadata$IID); bi <- match(b, metadata$IID)  # <8>
      same <- identical(unname(unlist(metadata[ai, c("SEX", "Age", "Disease")])),
                        unname(unlist(metadata[bi, c("SEX", "Age", "Disease")])))
      remove <- union(remove, if (same) lower_call_rate(a, b) else c(a, b))  # <9>
    }
  } else if (value > 0.177 && !a %in% remove && !b %in% remove) remove <- union(remove, lower_call_rate(a, b))  # <10>
}
remove_file <- guided_list(remove, guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "remove.txt"), TRUE)  # <11>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.5"), "--remove", remove_file, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.6")))  # <12>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.6", "3.5")
guided_register(cfg, "3.6", "3.5", 1920, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Choose the name for the report comparing pairs of samples.
2. Compare pairs using the selected variants.
3. Read the pairs and put the closest matches first.
4. Read the sample details, measure the missing data of every sample and start an empty removal list.
5. Review each pair to decide which samples to remove.
6. Treat the closest matches as repeated samples.
7. Remove the labelled repeat when its name ends in _R2.
8. Compare sex, age and disease status for unlabelled repeats.
9. Keep one matching record or remove both conflicting records.
10. Keep one person from each remaining closely related pair.
11. Write the removal list.
12. Save the dataset without the listed samples.

### What each option does

**Command 1: compare pairs of samples**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--extract` | Uses only the variants named in the supplied variant list. |
| `--make-king-table` | Estimates how closely related each pair of samples is and writes a table. |
| `--king-table-filter` | Writes only pairs whose kinship score is above 0.0442. The kinship score measures how closely two people are related. This value is an approximate boundary for third-degree relatives such as first cousins. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 2: measure the missing data of every sample**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--missing` | Measures the share of missing genotype calls and writes a table with one row per sample. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sample-only` | Writes only the sample table, not the variant table. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 3: remove repeated or closely related samples**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--remove` | Removes the samples named in the supplied sample list. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

There are 19 duplicate-class pairs and ten first-degree pairs. In total, 30 records are removed. 1,920 samples remain. Pairs can overlap, because one person can be in more than one pair. For this reason, the pair counts are not counts of unique people.

:::

::: {.callout-note title="PLINK terminal equivalent"}

These commands are shown for reference. Run the R chunk above to follow the course.
R creates any lists needed between PLINK commands. On Windows, use `bin\plink2.exe`.

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-5_state --extract results/guided/s3-4_prune.prune.in --make-king-table --king-table-filter 0.0442 --out results/guided/s3-6_king --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-5_state --missing sample-only --out results/guided/s3-6_missing --threads 2 --memory 2048
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-5_state --remove results/guided/s3-6_remove.txt --make-pgen --out results/guided/s3-6_state --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

:::

::: {.callout-tip title="Try other thresholds (optional)" collapse="true"}

This optional box is not part of the main path and does not change your results. The examples use simulated data, so the true answer is known ([why](../lessons/module_05_population_structure.Rmd#step-5-1)).

The usual KING cutoffs are 0.354 for repeated samples, 0.177 for first-degree relatives, 0.0884 for second-degree and 0.0442 for third-degree relatives (Manichaikul et al. 2010, [doi:10.1093/bioinformatics/btq559](https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/btq559)). The trials change the cutoff for relatives.

**Chart: KING kinship cutoff.**

**Why this simulation.** Related people break the assumption that samples are independent. Which kinship cutoff should we use?

**How to read the chart.** Each point is one kinship cutoff for relatives. The vertical axis counts the samples removed, and the diamond is the course value. Pairs above 0.354 are always treated as repeats of one sample.

**Try this: change the value in the R chunk and run it again.**

- Change the setting to **0.0442**. Note the count.
- Change it to **0.354**. Fewer samples are removed, because close relatives stay.

**What you should see, and why.** In this simulated cohort no pair lies between 0.0442 and 0.177, so the first three cutoffs remove the same samples. Real cohorts have more distant relatives, so their counts would differ.

**Why it matters for your GWAS.** [step 3.6](../lessons/module_03_sample_quality_control.Rmd#step-3-6) removes one sample of each related pair. Close relatives share alleles, and keeping them inflates the tests.

**Key idea:** The cutoff decides which degree of relatedness the cohort accepts.

```{r}
#| label: s3-6_thresholds
#| eval: false
# Optional. The trials use the table of pairs that the step wrote. No PLINK run is needed.
cutoffs <- c(0.0442, 0.0884, 0.177, 0.354)
kin <- guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "king"), ".kin0"))
trial <- data.frame(threshold = cutoffs, removed = kinship_counts(kin, guided_metadata(cfg), cutoffs, guided_table(paste0(guided_path(cfg, "3.6", "missing"), ".smiss"))))
trial$course_value <- trial$threshold == 0.177
trial
# Plot the removed samples. The course value is the large diamond.
plot_threshold_trials(trial, "Samples removed")
# Optional: add engine = "ggplot2" to plot_threshold_trials() to draw the plot with ggplot2 (install.packages("ggplot2") once first).
```


Plain PLINK 2 command for one trial. It writes only small files with the name that you give to `--out`, never a new dataset:

```sh
bin/plink2 --pfile results/guided/s3-5_state --extract results/guided/s3-4_prune.prune.in --king-cutoff 0.177 --out results/trials/s3-6_trial --threads 2 --memory 2048
```

`--king-cutoff` removes one member of each pair above the cutoff and writes two lists of sample IDs. Its count can differ a little from the course rule, which treats repeats separately.

The expected result of the trials:

| Kinship cutoff | Samples removed | Samples remaining |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 0.0442 | 30 | 1,920 |
| 0.0884 | 30 | 1,920 |
| **0.177 (course value)** | 30 | 1,920 |
| 0.354 | 20 | 1,930 |

:::

## Step 3.7 · Batch effects {#step-3-7}

We compare the fraction of successful genotype calls across laboratory plates. We remove the faulty plate in these simulated data because samples processed together can share technical problems.

[Read step 3.7 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-7).

```{r}
#| label: s3-7
report <- guided_path(cfg, "3.7", "missing")  # <1>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.6"), "--missing", "sample-only", "--out", report))  # <2>
missing <- guided_table(paste0(report, ".smiss"))  # <3>
metadata <- guided_metadata(cfg)
plate <- metadata$Plate[match(missing$IID, metadata$IID)]
median_missing <- tapply(as.numeric(missing$F_MISS), plate, median)  # <4>
print(sort(1 - median_missing))
worst <- names(which.max(median_missing))  # <5>
stopifnot(worst == "P14")
remove_file <- guided_list(missing$IID[plate == worst], guided_path(cfg, "3.7", "remove.txt"), TRUE)  # <6>
run_plink(cfg, c("--pfile", guided_path(cfg, "3.6"), "--remove", remove_file, "--make-pgen", "--out", guided_path(cfg, "3.7")))  # <7>
# Course bookkeeping: records the counts for the next step. Do not change.
ops <- guided_replay_lists(cfg, "3.7", "3.6")
guided_register(cfg, "3.7", "3.6", 1844, 296360, operations = ops)
```

1. Choose the name for the missing-call report.
2. Count missing calls for each sample.
3. Read the report and match each sample to its laboratory plate.
4. Calculate and print the middle call rate for each plate.
5. Find the plate with the most missing calls and check its name.
6. Write the list of samples from the faulty plate.
7. Save the dataset without samples from that plate.

### What each option does

**Command 1: measure missing calls by sample**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--missing` | Writes a report of missing genotype calls. |
| &nbsp;&nbsp;&rarr; `sample-only` | Writes one row per sample and skips the report for variants. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

**Command 2: remove samples from the faulty plate**

| Option or modifier | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `--pfile` | Reads the PGEN, PVAR and PSAM input files that share the given name prefix. |
| `--remove` | Removes the samples named in the supplied sample list. |
| `--make-pgen` | Saves a new dataset as PGEN, PVAR and PSAM files. |
| `--out` | Sets the shared beginning of the output file names. |

Every command also uses `--threads 2` (PLINK runs at most two tasks at the same time) and `--memory 2048` (PLINK uses at most about 2 GB of memory).

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Plate P14 has a median call rate of approximately 98.56%. The other plates have 99.84%. The 76 remaining wells of plate P14 are removed. 1,844 samples and 296,360 variants remain.

## Step 3.8 · Sample QC summary and checkpoint {#step-3-8}

We save the complete dataset after sample quality control and review the recorded counts. This gives us a checked starting point for variant quality control in module 4.

[Read step 3.8 on the course website](https://www.manuelgentiluomo.it/teaching/gwas/module-3/step-3-8).

```{r}
#| label: s3-8
guided_snapshot(cfg, "3.8", guided_path(cfg, "3.7"), 1844, 296360, parent = "3.7")  # <1>
print(read.delim(file.path(cfg$out, "step_counts.tsv")))  # <2>
check_step("3.8", data_dir = cfg$out, work_dir = cfg$out)  # <3>
```

1. Save a complete copy of the dataset after sample checks.
2. Print the recorded sample and variant counts.
3. Check that the saved files have the expected counts.

### What each option does

No PLINK options are used in this step.

::: {.callout-tip title="Expected result" collapse="true"}

Module 3 boundary: 1,844 samples and 296,360 variants. The restart operations for the steps in between are stored. The complete main-path package supplies full genotype copies at steps 2.8, 3.8, 4.6 and 5.7. Steps 4.6 and 5.7 are the ends of later modules. You can rebuild the states in between from the previous full checkpoint and the stored replay operations. To restart, give R the first step that you will run, for example `restore_checkpoint("4.1")` to start module 4. Use an empty output folder.

:::

No PLINK equivalent
